AI or human agent? When AI replies, when it only drafts, and when it hands off

The real question isn't whether AI should talk to your customers. It's which conversations it handles alone, which it only drafts, and which it shouldn't touch at all.

LVBy Lucas Vaz·October 28, 2026·8 min read

Key takeaways

  • There are three modes, not two: AI replies on its own, AI drafts a reply for someone to approve, or the chat goes straight to a person.
  • Pick the mode by the cost of a mistake and the need for judgment, not by how often a topic comes up.
  • Start in draft mode for two weeks. It shows exactly where the AI gets things right before it speaks alone.
  • A topic moves to automatic replies only when nearly all its drafts are approved without edits.
  • Meta's policy requires a clear path for customers to reach a person. Make it easy instead of hiding it.

Monday, 8:15 am. The receptionist at a dental office opens her computer to 34 conversations from the weekend. Twenty-two are some version of “how much is teeth whitening?” and “do you take insurance X?”. Eight are appointment requests. Three are complaints. One is from a patient whose face has been swollen since Saturday.

If an AI had answered everything alone, the first 22 would be done. But the swollen face can't get the same automatic reply as the whitening question.

That's the heart of the AI or human agent question. In practice, the answer is deciding, topic by topic, who talks to the customer and with how much oversight.

The three modes: reply, draft or hand off

Many people think of AI as a switch: on or off. In practice there are three modes, and most businesses use all three at once.

  • Replies on its own. The AI reads the message and answers in seconds, with no one reviewing. Best for questions with a known answer and low risk.
  • Drafts a reply. The AI writes the answer, but it waits until someone on the team reads, adjusts and sends it. The agent saves time; the customer gets a reviewed reply.
  • Hands off to a person. The AI doesn't answer the substance. At most, it tells the customer someone will take over and leaves a summary for the team.

The middle mode is the most overlooked, and it's the one that makes rollout safe. More on it below.

This guide is about who replies. For how the AI should talk (tone, knowledge, instructions), there's a separate guide on using AI on WhatsApp without sounding like a robot.

How to decide: two questions for each type of conversation

The temptation is to decide by volume: “this comes up a lot, so the AI should answer it”. Volume helps you prioritize, but it doesn't pick the mode. Two questions do.

1. What does a mistake cost here? If the AI gets your opening hours wrong, the customer shows up to a locked door. Annoying, but fixable. If it gives the wrong guidance to a patient with swelling, or promises a refund the business won't honor, the damage is of a different kind.

2. Does the answer need judgment or just information? “How much is a check-up?” is information: it's on the price list. “Can I get a discount if I book three sessions?” needs judgment: it depends on your schedule, your margin, the customer.

Put them together:

  • Cheap mistake, information only: AI replies on its own.
  • Moderate mistake, or information that varies case by case: AI drafts, a person approves.
  • Costly mistake, or it needs judgment, empathy or authority: a person takes over.

The decision matrix by type of conversation

This table is a starting point for most businesses serving customers on WhatsApp. Copy it, adjust it for your case, and pin it on the wall.

Type of conversationModeWhy
Hours, address, payment methodsAI aloneFixed info, cheap mistake
List prices, catalog, shippingAI aloneIt's on the list you taught it
Appointment requestAI alone or draftDepends on an up-to-date calendar
Custom quoteDraftFigures vary case by case
Order or delivery statusDraftNeeds checking the real info
Simple return or exchangeDraftClear policy, but every case has details
Discount or special termsPersonNeeds authority
ComplaintPersonNeeds empathy and a decision
Payments, billing, refundsPersonMistakes cost money and trust
Health, legal, safetyPersonMistakes can cause real harm
Customer asks for a personPerson, right awayAlways. No debate

Notice that “custom quote” sits in draft, not with a person. The AI builds 80% of the reply (items, reference prices, standard lead time) and the salesperson just checks and adjusts. That's where draft mode saves the most time.

What a handoff to a person should sound like

In a handoff, the customer needs to understand what happened and when they'll hear back. And they should never have to repeat their story.

There's also a rule behind this. The WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy allows automation when replying within the 24-hour window, but requires businesses to offer prompt, clear and direct escalation paths to a person, such as an in-chat transfer to a human agent, a phone number or email. Hiding the human behind a maze of menus goes against the rule.

A few handoff messages that work:

Got it. Requests like this are handled by Sarah on our sales team. I've passed it to her with a summary of our chat. She'll get back to you today, before 5 pm.

I'm sorry about that. I'm bringing in someone from the team right now to handle your case personally. No need to explain again, I've noted everything.

From what you describe, it's best to speak with the dentist. I've already alerted the team and they'll call you shortly. If the pain gets worse or you have a fever, please go to urgent care.

On the inside, the summary your team receives should have three lines: who the customer is, what they want, what's already been said. Something like “Mark, patient since 2024. Wants to move his braces adjustment from Thursday to Saturday. AI said there's a 10 am slot on Saturday but didn't confirm.”

Roll it out in phases: start with drafts

The most common mistake is switching the AI to automatic for everything on day one and discovering the problems through complaints. A phased rollout avoids that.

Weeks 1 and 2: everything in draft

The AI writes, the team approves. Nobody is served more slowly than before, because the reply arrives ready-made. And you get valuable material: you can see exactly where the AI gets it right, where it's wrong and why. Every corrected draft is a piece of information missing from its knowledge.

Weeks 3 and 4: automatic for routine topics

Pick the three or four topics where drafts were almost always approved without edits (hours, list prices, address, payment methods) and let the AI reply on its own for those only. Everything else stays in draft.

Month two onward: expand with care

Every two weeks, review the numbers and move one or two more topics to automatic. Some will never leave draft mode, and that's fine. The topics in the “person” column stay with people.

In Kontaro, the AI can reply automatically or write a draft for someone to approve, and you test its answers before turning it on. When it hands off, the team gets the history and a summary in the same inbox.

How to tell whether the split is working

You don't need a complex dashboard. Five numbers, checked once a week, tell you almost everything:

  1. Drafts approved without edits. By topic. It's your gauge for switching to automatic.
  2. Conversations handed to the team. If this rises for no reason, the AI is missing knowledge.
  3. Customers who asked for a person. If many do, the AI is annoying people, even when it's right.
  4. Reopened conversations. The customer came back because the answer didn't solve it.
  5. Time to first reply. It should drop sharply on automatic topics.

A hypothetical example to illustrate. In week two, a store had 200 drafts about prices and shipping. 184 were sent without any change (92%), 12 had small tweaks and 4 were rewritten because the shipping table for one region was out of date. Once the table is fixed, it makes sense to move that topic to automatic. Drafts about order status, on the other hand, had a 60% no-edit approval rate: they stay in draft.

My rule of thumb, backed by nothing but experience: I only move a topic to automatic once it passes 90% no-edit approval for two weeks in a row. For the numbers worth tracking across your whole support operation, see the guide to customer service metrics that matter.

And set aside 20 minutes a week to read real AI conversations. Numbers show trends, but only reading shows a reply that's technically correct and has the wrong tone.

Mistakes that make AI look worse than it is

  • Hiding the option to talk to a person. A customer who needs someone will keep insisting, and every extra message adds frustration.
  • Handing off without context. The agent opens with “how can I help?” and the customer has to tell the whole story again.
  • Handing off to a queue nobody watches. The AI says someone will reply, and nobody does. That's worse than having no AI. Nights and weekends need their own routine, which I cover in the guide to after-hours customer service.
  • Never revisiting the modes. What was right in March may not be in October: prices change, policies change, the team changes.

Start tomorrow with a sheet of paper

Before touching any settings, take your last 50 WhatsApp conversations and label each with a letter: A (AI could answer alone), D (draft), P (person). It takes half an hour.

You'll find two things. First, the A column is bigger than it seemed. Second, a few P conversations are currently waiting in the same queue as questions about opening hours. Separating the two improves your service on its own, with or without AI.

Frequently asked questions

Do customers prefer talking to AI or to a human agent?

Most want a correct, fast answer, whoever gives it. Frustration starts when the AI gets things wrong, sticks to a script, or blocks the customer from reaching a person. That's why the path to a human has to be easy.

When should AI hand a conversation off to a person?

When the customer asks, when the AI doesn't have the information, and on topics where a mistake is costly: complaints, payments, discounts, health, legal matters. The handoff should include a summary so the customer doesn't repeat everything.

What is AI draft mode?

The AI writes the reply, but someone on the team reads it, adjusts it if needed and sends it. It's a safe way to train the AI and a good fit for topics where you want speed without giving up review.

Does Meta allow AI on WhatsApp?

Yes. The WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy allows automated replies, as long as customers have clear, direct ways to reach a person, such as an in-chat transfer to an agent, a phone number or email.
